title: Search Insert Position
summary: You get a list of integers `nums`, sorted from smallest to largest with no repeats, and an integer `target`. If `target` is in `nums`, return its index. If it isn't, return the index where you would insert it so that `nums` stays sorted. Your search should take O(log n) time, where n is the length of `nums`.

examples.explanation: 5 isn't in the list. It fits between 0 and 7, so inserting it at index 2 keeps the list sorted.
12 is already in the list, at index 3.
20 is bigger than every number, so it goes after the last one: index 3, one past the end.

constraints: Each number in nums is bigger than the one before it

approaches.twist: Return lo when the target is missing: the loop leaves it where the target should be inserted.
Walk from the left and return the index of the first number at least as big as the target, or the length of nums if there is none.
approaches.note: Works, but it may read every number, so it takes O(n) time. The target is O(log n).

signals.meaning: Sorted order means the middle value tells you which side of it target belongs on, so you can drop the other side without reading it.
A scan reads every number, which is O(n). To reach log n, each step has to halve the part of nums that's still in play.
That's the first index whose number is at least target: everything before it is smaller. bisect.bisect_left returns exactly that index.

constraintReading: len(nums) is at most 10⁴, so even reading every number would be fast: the size alone allows O(n). The O(log n) time target is what rules out a scan. Halving the range takes at most 14 checks for 10⁴ numbers, and the O(1) space target means you keep two indexes, not a copy of nums.

hints.clarify: What do you return when `target` is already in `nums`, and what when it's smaller or bigger than every number? Try [4, 10, 16] by hand. A target of 10 gives 1, its own index. 13 isn't there, but it fits between 10 and 16, so it gives 2. A target of 1 would go first, at index 0, and 25 would go last, at index 3: one past the end.
hints.approach: Binary search with a different ending. `nums` is sorted, so the middle value tells you which side `target` belongs on. Keep `lo` and `hi` at the edges of the range still in play, check the middle, and move one edge past it. If the middle equals `target`, return its index. If the loop ends without a match, look at where it stopped: every number left of `lo` is smaller than `target`, every number right of `hi` is bigger, and `lo` is now just past `hi`. So `lo` is exactly where `target` belongs. Each check halves the range, so 10⁴ numbers take at most 14 checks.
hints.whyNot: A scan from the left that stops at the first number at least as big as `target` gives the right index, but it may read all n numbers: O(n) time, and the target is O(log n). Also watch the ending. A plain binary search returns -1 when the loop runs out, but here the answer is left behind in `lo`. Don't return `hi`, which stops one index before the insert position, or `mid`, which is wherever the last check happened.

slots.setup: `lo` at 0 and `hi` at the last index. At the start, `target` could belong anywhere, even one past the end.
slots.loop: Keep going while `lo` is at most `hi`, so at least one index is left to check. Each round, set `mid` halfway between them, rounded down.
slots.update: If the value at `mid` is smaller than `target`, `target` belongs after it: move `lo` to the index just after `mid`. If it's bigger, move `hi` to the index just before `mid`.
slots.record: Compare the value at `mid` with `target`. If they're equal, `target` is already in `nums`: return `mid`.
slots.return: When the loop ends, `lo` is one past `hi`. Every number before `lo` is smaller than `target` and every number from `lo` on is bigger, so return `lo`. It can be one past the last index.

solution.explanation: Each round either returns or halves the range from `lo` to `hi`, so n numbers need at most log₂ n + 1 rounds: O(log n) time. Only `lo`, `hi` and `mid` are stored, so the space is O(1). Why `lo` is the answer when `target` is missing: every move keeps the numbers left of `lo` smaller than `target` and the numbers right of `hi` bigger. The loop ends with `lo` one past `hi`, so `lo` is the first index whose number is bigger than `target`, or one past the end if none is: exactly where `target` goes. Python's `bisect_left` returns the same index.

events.label: check
events.say: The middle is ({lo} + {hi}) // 2 = {mid}, and nums[{mid}] is {nums[mid]}

events.label: go right
events.say: {nums[mid]} is less than {target}, so it and everything before it are too small: search to the right

events.label: go left
events.say: {nums[mid]} is more than {target}, so it and everything after it are too big: search to the left

events.label: found
events.say: nums[{mid}] is {target}, so it's already in the list: return {mid}

events.label: insert
events.say: lo = {lo} has passed hi = {hi}, so {target} is missing. Every number before index {lo} is smaller and the rest are bigger: return {lo}

predict.ask: hi is about to move below mid. Is mid itself where the target belongs?

related.relation: Same loop on a sorted list, but a missing target returns -1 instead of the index where lo stops.
Also leaves lo on the first spot that passes a test, but the spots are eating speeds, and each test adds up hours over all the piles.
